Hypotonic sodium loss causing hypotonic contraction
Excess isotonic saline causing isosmotic expansion
Pure intracellular solute gain without water loss
choice_rationales: Absent intake produces a water deficit relative to sodium, raising serum sodium and tonicity while contracting body water.

Isotonic sodium loss causing isosmotic contraction does not account for the complete displayed pattern. The elevated sodium requires a relative water deficit rather than an isotonic loss or isotonic gain.

Voltage-mediated distal type 1 RTA with impaired H⁺ and K⁺ excretion does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Proximal RTA has urine pH that varies with serum bicarbonate, type 4 and voltage-mediated distal RTA are hyperkalemic, and an appropriate response to extrarenal bicarbonate loss increases urinary NH₄Cl rather than leaving a positive urine anion gap.

Appropriate renal response to an extrarenal bicarbonate loss does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Proximal RTA has urine pH that varies with serum bicarbonate, type 4 and voltage-mediated distal RTA are hyperkalemic, and an appropriate response to extrarenal bicarbonate loss increases urinary NH₄Cl rather than leaving a positive urine anion gap.

questions.tested_concept: Proximal type 2 RTA from impaired HCO₃⁻ reclamation
questions.stem: A patient with a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis is evaluated at two different serum bicarbonate concentrations. Which tubular defect best explains the changing urine pH?
questions.visual_target: Integrate the primary clinical data table with the case context to select the only fully concordant conclusion.
options: Classic distal type 1 RTA from failure of distal H⁺ secretion
Type 4 RTA from low aldosterone and impaired NH₄⁺ buffering
Proximal type 2 RTA from impaired HCO₃⁻ reclamation
Voltage-mediated distal type 1 RTA with impaired H⁺ and K⁺ excretion
Appropriate renal response to an extrarenal bicarbonate loss
choice_rationales: Classic distal type 1 RTA from failure of distal H⁺ secretion does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Persistently alkaline urine favors distal acidification failure, hyperkalemia favors type 4 or voltage-mediated disease, and an extrarenal bicarbonate loss does not create a proximal reclamation threshold pattern.

Type 4 RTA from low aldosterone and impaired NH₄⁺ buffering does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Persistently alkaline urine favors distal acidification failure, hyperkalemia favors type 4 or voltage-mediated disease, and an extrarenal bicarbonate loss does not create a proximal reclamation threshold pattern.

In proximal type 2 RTA, bicarbonate spills into urine while the filtered load exceeds the reduced reclamation threshold, but the intact distal nephron can lower urine pH once serum bicarbonate falls. The lecture also associates type 2 RTA with hypokalemia.

Voltage-mediated distal type 1 RTA with impaired H⁺ and K⁺ excretion does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Persistently alkaline urine favors distal acidification failure, hyperkalemia favors type 4 or voltage-mediated disease, and an extrarenal bicarbonate loss does not create a proximal reclamation threshold pattern.

Appropriate renal response to an extrarenal bicarbonate loss does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Persistently alkaline urine favors distal acidification failure, hyperkalemia favors type 4 or voltage-mediated disease, and an extrarenal bicarbonate loss does not create a proximal reclamation threshold pattern.
questions.explanation: In proximal type 2 RTA, bicarbonate spills into urine while the filtered load exceeds the reduced reclamation threshold, but the intact distal nephron can lower urine pH once serum bicarbonate falls. The lecture also associates type 2 RTA with hypokalemia.
visual_clues: Urine pH changes with serum bicarbonate
Hypokalemia with a variable urine anion gap

questions.tested_concept: Type 4 RTA with hyperkalemia reducing NH₃ availability and therefore NH₄⁺ excretion
questions.stem: A patient with a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis has evidence of reduced aldosterone activity. Which mechanism best explains the acidosis despite the acidic urine pH?
questions.visual_target: Integrate the primary clinical data table with the case context to select the only fully concordant conclusion.
options: Classic distal type 1 RTA from failure of distal H⁺ secretion
Proximal type 2 RTA from impaired HCO₃⁻ reclamation
Voltage-mediated distal type 1 RTA with loss of the negative lumen potential
Type 4 RTA with hyperkalemia reducing NH₃ availability and therefore NH₄⁺ excretion
Appropriate renal response to an extrarenal bicarbonate loss
choice_rationales: Classic distal type 1 RTA from failure of distal H⁺ secretion does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Classic distal RTA has persistently high urine pH, proximal RTA has variable urine pH with hypokalemia, voltage-mediated distal RTA also impairs luminal H⁺ secretion, and an appropriate extrarenal response increases NH₄Cl excretion.

Proximal type 2 RTA from impaired HCO₃⁻ reclamation does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Classic distal RTA has persistently high urine pH, proximal RTA has variable urine pH with hypokalemia, voltage-mediated distal RTA also impairs luminal H⁺ secretion, and an appropriate extrarenal response increases NH₄Cl excretion.

Voltage-mediated distal type 1 RTA with loss of the negative lumen potential does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Classic distal RTA has persistently high urine pH, proximal RTA has variable urine pH with hypokalemia, voltage-mediated distal RTA also impairs luminal H⁺ secretion, and an appropriate extrarenal response increases NH₄Cl excretion.

Type 4 RTA is hyperkalemic and linked to low aldosterone activity. High potassium reduces ammonia buffering, so net ammonium excretion is low and the urine anion gap stays positive even though free H⁺ can lower urine pH below 5.5.

Appropriate renal response to an extrarenal bicarbonate loss does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Classic distal RTA has persistently high urine pH, proximal RTA has variable urine pH with hypokalemia, voltage-mediated distal RTA also impairs luminal H⁺ secretion, and an appropriate extrarenal response increases NH₄Cl excretion.
questions.explanation: Type 4 RTA is hyperkalemic and linked to low aldosterone activity. High potassium reduces ammonia buffering, so net ammonium excretion is low and the urine anion gap stays positive even though free H⁺ can lower urine pH below 5.5.
visual_clues: High serum K⁺ with low aldosterone effect
Acidic urine but a positive urine anion gap

questions.tested_concept: Voltage-mediated distal type 1 RTA with impaired H⁺ and K⁺ excretion
questions.stem: A patient develops a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis after loss of the normal negative electrical potential in the distal tubular lumen. Which RTA subtype and transport consequence best fit this pattern?
questions.visual_target: Integrate the primary clinical data table with the case context to select the only fully concordant conclusion.
options: Classic distal type 1 RTA with hypokalemia from isolated H⁺ pump failure
Proximal type 2 RTA from impaired HCO₃⁻ reclamation
Type 4 RTA with preserved ability to lower urine pH
Appropriate renal response to an extrarenal bicarbonate loss
Voltage-mediated distal type 1 RTA with impaired H⁺ and K⁺ excretion
choice_rationales: Classic distal type 1 RTA with hypokalemia from isolated H⁺ pump failure does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Classic pump failure is usually hypokalemic, proximal RTA has bicarbonate-dependent urine pH, type 4 RTA usually retains the ability to lower urine pH below 5.5, and extrarenal loss should increase urinary NH₄Cl excretion.

Proximal type 2 RTA from impaired HCO₃⁻ reclamation does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Classic pump failure is usually hypokalemic, proximal RTA has bicarbonate-dependent urine pH, type 4 RTA usually retains the ability to lower urine pH below 5.5, and extrarenal loss should increase urinary NH₄Cl excretion.

Type 4 RTA with preserved ability to lower urine pH does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Classic pump failure is usually hypokalemic, proximal RTA has bicarbonate-dependent urine pH, type 4 RTA usually retains the ability to lower urine pH below 5.5, and extrarenal loss should increase urinary NH₄Cl excretion.

Appropriate renal response to an extrarenal bicarbonate loss does not account for the complete displayed pattern. Classic pump failure is usually hypokalemic, proximal RTA has bicarbonate-dependent urine pH, type 4 RTA usually retains the ability to lower urine pH below 5.5, and extrarenal loss should increase urinary NH₄Cl excretion.

Loss of the negative distal lumen potential removes the electrical drive for both H⁺ and K⁺ secretion. The result is hyperkalemic distal type 1 RTA with persistently alkaline urine and a positive urine anion gap.
questions.explanation: Loss of the negative distal lumen potential removes the electrical drive for both H⁺ and K⁺ secretion. The result is hyperkalemic distal type 1 RTA with persistently alkaline urine and a positive urine anion gap.
visual_clues: Loss of the negative distal lumen potential
Both H⁺ and K⁺ excretion are impaired

choice_rationales: Autonomous aldosterone raises distal sodium reabsorption and potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing low-renin hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: A patient with systemic lupus features develops combined nephritic and nephrotic renal findings. Which renal immune-deposit pattern most strongly supports the diagnosis?
questions.visual_target: Integrate the primary clinical data table with the case context to select the only fully concordant conclusion.
options: Anti-GBM disease with isolated linear IgG
Minimal change disease with negative immunofluorescence
Lupus nephritis with granular full-house immunofluorescence
Acute tubular necrosis with muddy brown casts
choice_rationales: Anti-GBM disease with isolated linear IgG does not account for the complete displayed pattern. The systemic autoimmune context and combined nephritic-nephrotic presentation require immune-complex glomerular disease rather than podocyte or tubular injury.

Minimal change disease with negative immunofluorescence does not account for the complete displayed pattern. The systemic autoimmune context and combined nephritic-nephrotic presentation require immune-complex glomerular disease rather than podocyte or tubular injury.

FSGS with no immune deposits does not account for the complete displayed pattern. The systemic autoimmune context and combined nephritic-nephrotic presentation require immune-complex glomerular disease rather than podocyte or tubular injury.
Lupus nephritis is an immune-complex glomerulonephritis with broad immunoglobulin and complement deposition, producing the characteristic full-house granular pattern.

Acute tubular necrosis with muddy brown casts does not account for the complete displayed pattern. The systemic autoimmune context and combined nephritic-nephrotic presentation require immune-complex glomerular disease rather than podocyte or tubular injury.
questions.explanation: Lupus nephritis is an immune-complex glomerulonephritis with broad immunoglobulin and complement deposition, producing the characteristic full-house granular pattern.

questions.tested_concept: Regenerating acute tubular injury with mitoses and casts, followed by a diuretic phase that risks volume and electrolyte loss
questions.stem: A 48-year-old is pinned under a wall for four hours, arrives with BP 70/40 mm Hg, and produces only 300 mL urine in 24 hours; biopsy is obtained ten days later. Which biopsy phase and near-term complication should be anticipated?
questions.visual_target: Integrate the primary clinical data table with the case context to select the only fully concordant conclusion.
options: Anti-GBM crescent formation followed by pulmonary hemorrhage
Minimal change disease followed by selective proteinuria
Chronic pyelonephritis followed by persistent obstruction
Membranous nephropathy followed by renal-vein thrombosis
Regenerating acute tubular injury with mitoses and casts, followed by a diuretic phase that risks volume and electrolyte loss
choice_rationales: Anti-GBM crescent formation followed by pulmonary hemorrhage does not account for the complete displayed pattern. The shock, oliguria, and delayed biopsy timing fit ischemic tubular injury and regeneration rather than glomerular or chronic infectious disease.

Minimal change disease followed by selective proteinuria does not account for the complete displayed pattern. The shock, oliguria, and delayed biopsy timing fit ischemic tubular injury and regeneration rather than glomerular or chronic infectious disease.

Chronic pyelonephritis followed by persistent obstruction does not account for the complete displayed pattern. The shock, oliguria, and delayed biopsy timing fit ischemic tubular injury and regeneration rather than glomerular or chronic infectious disease.

Membranous nephropathy followed by renal-vein thrombosis does not account for the complete displayed pattern. The shock, oliguria, and delayed biopsy timing fit ischemic tubular injury and regeneration rather than glomerular or chronic infectious disease.
Severe ischemia causes ATN; by day ten, regenerating tubular epithelium and residual debris may precede a high-output recovery phase with hypovolemia, hyponatremia, and hypokalemia risk.
questions.explanation: Severe ischemia causes ATN; by day ten, regenerating tubular epithelium and residual debris may precede a high-output recovery phase with hypovolemia, hyponatremia, and hypokalemia risk.
visual_clues: Biopsy occurs ten days after injury

questions.stem: A dissected kidney contains irregular concretions in upper-pole calyces, including a branching calculus, with acute renal inflammation microscopically. Which stone composition and infection mechanism best unify the gross and microscopic findings?
questions.visual_target: Integrate the primary clinical data table with the case context to select the only fully concordant conclusion.

Uric-acid stone from acidic urine with sterile interstitium
Calcium oxalate stone that proves anti-GBM disease
Cystine stone caused by ADH excess
Drug crystal causing isolated minimal change disease
choice_rationales: A branching staghorn calculus is classically magnesium ammonium phosphate precipitated in alkaline urine from urease-producing organisms; obstruction favors ascending renal infection.
